cues.text: A Pagan King Among Arian Neighbors

By the late fifth century, Clovis , king of the Salian Franks since 481, had conquered most of Gaul north of the Loire, defeating the last Roman governor Syagrius and extending Frankish power to the Rhine.

Unlike the Visigoths, Burgundians, and Vandals who surrounded his kingdom — all Arian Christians who denied Christ's full divinity — Clovis himself remained a pagan, worshipping the old Germanic gods of his ancestors.
Clotilda's Influence
Around 492 Clovis married Clotilda , a devoutly Catholic Burgundian princess.
She worked for years to win her husband to the Catholic faith, first securing his consent to baptize their firstborn son, who died in infancy — a tragedy Clovis blamed on her God.
Undeterred, Clotilda persuaded him to allow the baptism of their second son as well, and continued to press her husband toward conversion.
The Battle of Tolbiac and the King's Vow
According to tradition preserved by Gregory of Tours, Clovis's decisive turn came during a desperate battle against the Alemanni, believed to be fought near Tolbiac.
Seeing his army on the point of collapse, Clovis is said to have cried out to the God of Clotilda for victory, vowing to be baptized if he prevailed.
The Franks routed the Alemanni, and Clovis kept his word.
The Baptism at Reims

On Christmas Day, 496 (some sources place it slightly later), St. Remigius , Bishop of Reims, baptized Clovis along with some three thousand of his warriors in a small church near what became the Abbey of Saint-Remi.
Later medieval legend embellished the ceremony with the miracle of the Holy Ampulla, a vial of chrism said to have been delivered from heaven by a dove for the anointing.
Tradition credits Remigius with a striking exhortation to the pagan king at the font, urging him to abandon the false gods he had followed and embrace the true faith he had until then persecuted.
Why the Baptism Mattered
Clovis's choice of orthodox, Nicene Catholicism rather than Arianism was of enormous consequence.
It aligned the Franks with the Gallo-Roman Catholic bishops and population already living under his rule.
This spared him from becoming an Arian overlord opposed to them, a crucial advantage his Arian rivals in Visigothic Spain and Ostrogothic Italy never enjoyed.
Catholic bishops, who had preserved much of Roman civic order in Gaul, now became Clovis's natural allies, lending his conquests both legitimacy and administrative sophistication.
Legacy: Eldest Daughter of the Church
The baptism of Clovis is traditionally regarded as the founding moment of Catholic France, later honored with the title fille aînée de l'Église —the 'eldest daughter of the Church.'
It secured the conversion of the Frankish people as a whole.
Gaul, soon to become the heartland of medieval Christendom, followed a Catholic rather than Arian trajectory.
The event was still commemorated as a national and religious milestone at its 1,500th anniversary in 1996, when Pope John Paul II visited Reims.
